### Google TPU 8 — What's New (April 22, 2026)
Two variants, same underlying platform (Arm Axion CPU, native FP4, JAX/PyTorch/XLA, 2× perf/watt vs. Ironwood):

| Feature | TPU 8t (Training) | TPU 8i (Inference) |
|---------|-------------------|---------------------|
| Workload | Large-scale pre-training | Inference, serving, reasoning |
| Network | 3D torus (9,600 chips/pod) | Boardfly (max 7 hops, 1,152 chips) |
| Special HW | SparseCore (embedding lookups) | CAE (collective acceleration) |
| HBM / SRAM | 216 GB / 128 MB | 288 GB / **384 MB (3× SRAM)** |
| Peak FP4 | **12.6 PFLOPs** | 10.1 PFLOPs |
| HBM BW | 6,528 GB/s | 8,601 GB/s (~1.3×) |
| vs. Ironwood | **2.7× training price-perf** | **80% inference price-perf** |

Key design insight: **8i trades raw compute for memory** — 3× more on-chip SRAM keeps the full KV cache on-chip for long-context inference without going to HBM. The Boardfly topology cuts latency 50% (7 hops vs. 16 in 3D torus) which matters for autoregressive decoding where each token is sequential.

> Pre-training is the first and most computationally expensive phase. TPU 7 consumed ~600 W.

## 1. How Can We Accelerate an Algorithm? (`w6_mon_transformers_in_memory.pdf`)

The core question: given a problem and hardware accelerator, how do we maximize **throughput**, minimize **latency** and **power**, while maintaining **reliability**?

### Traditional Techniques

| Optimization Technique | Potential Speedup | Difficulty | Applicability | Notes |
|----------------------|-------------------|------------|---------------|-------|
| Algorithm Selection | 10x–1000x+ | Medium–High | High | O(n²) → O(n log n) is massive at scale |
| Data Structure Optimization | 2x–100x | Medium | High | Hash tables vs. arrays for lookups |
| GPU Acceleration | 10x–1000x | High | Medium | Parallelizable computations only |
| Multithreading/Parallelization | 2x–64x | High | Medium | Capped by Amdahl's Law |
| Compiler Optimizations | 1.2x–4x | Low | High | Just change compiler flags |
| Memory Hierarchy Optimization | 2x–10x | Medium | High | Cache-friendly data structures |
| Memoization/Caching | 2x–100x | Low–Medium | Medium | Only for repeated calculations |
| Hardware Upgrade (CPU) | 1.5x–4x | Low | High | Generational improvement |
| SSD vs HDD Storage | 2x–100x | Low | Medium | I/O-bound algorithms only |
| FPGA/ASIC Implementation | 10x–1000x | **Very High** | Low | Custom HW, high dev cost |
| Code Micro-optimizations | 1.1x–2x | Medium | High | Loop unrolling, fewer function calls |
| Language Change (Interpreted→Compiled) | 3x–50x | High | Medium | Python → C++ |

### Processor Architecture Evolution (Mishra et al.)
Understanding how CPUs evolved shows why GPUs and systolic arrays exist:

1. **Simple processor** — 1 ALU, 1 integer op/cycle. The other ALU sits idle >99% of the time.
2. **FPU + ALU (Pentium)** — two execution units, out-of-order scheduler. One is still saturated; the other < 1% used.
3. **SMT — Simultaneous Multi-Threading** — 2 instruction streams share one core. Latency when one thread is blocked stalls both.
4. **SIMD — Vector Processing** — one instruction operates on multiple data words in parallel (4 adds at once). Same fundamental limitation as SMT for control-heavy code.
5. **SIMT — Single-Instruction Multiple-Threads** (GPU style) — hides memory latency by swapping threads on stall. Worse for algorithms that can't tolerate stalls well.
6. **AMD GCN / Modern GPU** — 4× SIMD + 1 ALU per compute unit + Warp Scheduler. SIMT + SIMD working together = how a modern GPU works.

**Takeaway**: each generation addressed one bottleneck but exposed another. The only escape is purpose-built hardware (TPU/systolic array) where the algorithm's structure matches the hardware's structure exactly.

## 2. No Free Lunch Theorem (NFL)

> Averaged over all possible problems, every optimization algorithm performs equally well. **No algorithm consistently outperforms random search.**

- Formalized by **Wolpert & Macready, 1997**
- Does NOT say all algorithms are equally good on your specific problem — it says there is no free universal winner

### Implications for HW/ML
- Specialized architectures (TPU, GPU, neuromorphic) excel in their domain but fail outside it
- **Domain knowledge is essential** when selecting algorithm or architecture
- **Any claim of superiority must specify the problem class** — "X is better than Y" without context is meaningless
- This is why FPGA/ASIC has the highest potential speedup but lowest applicability: it only wins when the algorithm perfectly matches the custom silicon

## 3. TPU Architecture — Recap

### MXU (Matrix Multiply Unit)
- **256 × 256 = 65,536 MACs per cycle**
- 8-bit integer (INT8) math
- Input: activations from **Unified Buffer** + weights from **Weight FIFO** (prefetched from DDR3 DRAM)
- Output: partial sums → **Accumulators** → **Activation** (ReLU etc.) → **Normalize/Pool**
- Connected to host via PCIe Gen3 x16 (14 GiB/s)

The **Weight FIFO** is the key: weights stream in continuously so the MXU is never stalled waiting for weights. Activations are stored locally in the Unified Buffer (on-chip SRAM). This is **weight-stationary** dataflow.

---

## 4. Systolic Array — Recap

- Name comes from the heart analogy: data "pulses" rhythmically through PEs
- CPUs/GPUs spend energy accessing multiple registers per operation
- Systolic array chains ALUs so **one register read feeds many MAC operations** — minimal data movement
- Structure: 2D grid of MACs; activations flow left→right, weights stay stationary (TPU), partial sums accumulate downward

### Mapping a DNN on a Systolic Array
```
Weight Memory (on-chip SRAM)
        ↓ preloaded weights w₁₁...wNN
[Activation Memory] → MAC(w₁₁) → MAC(w₂₁) → ... → MAC(wN₁)  → Activations out
                    → MAC(w₁₂) → MAC(w₂₂) → ... → MAC(wN₂)
                    → ...
                    → MAC(w₁N) → ...        → ... → MAC(wNN)
                         ↓           ↓                   ↓
                    [Accumulators: partial sums y₁₁,y₂₁,...,yNB]
```
Each MAC unit: 8-bit activation (a) × 8-bit weight (w) → 16-bit product → add to 24-bit accumulator output.

## 5. Transformers

### What Is a Transformer?
> "A transformer model is a neural network that learns context and thus meaning by **tracking relationships in sequential data** like the words in this sentence."

Key properties (improvements over RNNs):
- Fixes **all RNN/LSTM drawbacks**: vanishing gradients, sequential bottleneck, poor long-range dependencies
- **No labels needed** — self-supervised training on raw text
- **Very parallelizable** — all tokens processed simultaneously during training
- **Higher performance** at scale than any prior architecture

Structure: **encoder/decoder** = compression/decompression blocks. The encoder reads and compresses input; the decoder generates output conditioned on that compressed representation.

### Why NOT Recurrent?
RNNs/LSTMs process one token at a time — hidden state passes from step t to t+1:
- **Cannot parallelize** across time during training
- **Hidden state bottleneck** — all prior context crammed into a fixed vector
- **Vanishing gradients** over long sequences

Transformers replace recurrence **entirely with self-attention**:
- All tokens processed **in parallel**
- Every token connects **directly** to every other token — no propagation needed
- **No hidden state** — order encoded via positional encoding (sine/cosine), not time steps

### How Does a Transformer Learn? (Self-Supervised Pre-Training)
```
Text corpus → Tokenize → [The][cat][sat][?][the][mat]
                                              ↓
                                   Transformer Block (N layers)
                                              ↓
                                    Predict: "on"   (cross-entropy loss)
                                              ↓
                              Backprop: adjust weights to minimize loss
```

What it learns with **no human labels**:
- **Syntax and grammar** — word order, agreement, parts of speech
- **World knowledge** — facts, entities, common sense from text
- **Reasoning patterns** — inference, analogy, cause and effect

The key: the next word in the text is always the label. Billions of free training signals from any corpus.

### RLHF — Aligning Transformers with Human Feedback
After pre-training, the model is steered toward helpful/harmless/honest behavior in three stages:

1. **Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT)** — fine-tune pretrained LLM on human-written prompt+response demos. Output: initialized policy that knows what "good" looks like.

2. **Reward Model Training** — SFT generates response pairs A and B; humans rank which is better. Train a Reward Model (RM) via cross-entropy on these ranked pairs. Output: scalar score r(x,y).

3. **PPO RL Fine-Tuning** — Policy LLM generates response y; RM scores it; PPO updates the policy to maximize:
   ```
   Max E[r(x,y)] − β·KL(policy, SFT)
   ```
   The **KL penalty** prevents reward hacking — keeps the policy from drifting too far from the SFT baseline.

Key insight: humans rank outputs more easily than they write perfect ones. RLHF converts comparative preferences into reward signals.

> PPO = Proximal Policy Optimization · RM = Reward Model · KL = Kullback-Leibler divergence

### Main Mathematical Operations of a Transformer

| Operation | Hardware | Notes |
|-----------|----------|-------|
| **Matrix Multiplication** | Tensor cores / MXU | Dominant operation; used in attention AND FFN |
| **Q·Kᵀ / √d_k (Scaled dot-product)** | Tensor cores | `[GPU SFU]` for the scaling step |
| **Softmax** | CUDA core (SFU) | exp() is expensive; converts scores → probabilities |
| **Multi-head attention** | Tensor cores | H parallel attention ops concatenated |
| **Layer Normalization** | CUDA core | Normalizes per-feature using mean + variance |
| **Residual connections** | CUDA core | Addition; critical for gradient flow |
| **FFN (2× linear + ReLU)** | Tensor cores | Position-wise; same weights applied to all tokens |
| **Positional Encoding** | Pre-compute (one-time) | Sine/cosine at different frequencies `[GPU SFU]` |
| **Embedding** | Memory lookup | Tokens → continuous vectors |

**Attention formula**:
```
Attention(Q, K, V) = softmax(Q·Kᵀ / √d_k) · V
```
- `Q = X·Wq`, `K = X·Wk`, `V = X·Wv` (learned linear projections)
- Q: "What am I looking for?"
- K: "What do I offer?"
- V: "What do I actually contribute if selected?"

**Softmax formula**:
```
s(xᵢ) = e^xᵢ / Σⱼ e^xⱼ
```
All outputs positive, sum to exactly 1. Used to convert raw attention scores into a probability distribution over tokens.

### What Learns vs. What Is Fixed

| Component | Status | Details |
|-----------|--------|---------|
| Token embedding (W_e) | **Learned** | Lookup table: token ID → dense vector |
| Positional encoding | Fixed | sin/cos formulas, no parameters |
| W_Q, W_K, W_V | **Learned** | Linear projections for attention |
| Scaled dot-product (QKᵀ/√d_k) | Fixed | Operation, not a parameter |
| Softmax | Fixed | Fixed nonlinearity |
| W_O (output projection) | **Learned** | Projects concatenated heads back to d_model |
| Layer norm γ/β | **Learned** | Scale and shift (2 params per feature) |
| FFN weights W_1, W_2 | **Learned** | The two linear layers in each block |
| Activation (GELU/SwiGLU) | Fixed | Fixed nonlinearity |
| Unembedding / LM head (W_u) | **Learned** | Projects d_model → vocab size for token probs |

### Mapping Transformers on a GPU
All major operations are **GEMM** (General Matrix Multiply):
- Q, K, V projections: `X × Wm,Q`, `X × Wm,K`, `X × Wm,V`
- Attention: `Km^T × Qm` (MatMul), scale, softmax, then `× Vm` (MatMul)
- Output projection: `Zm × Wm`
- Add & Norm at each sub-layer

These map directly to tensor cores. Softmax and layer norm are non-GEMM and run on CUDA SFUs — they are a smaller fraction of compute but still critical to optimize.

## Key Formulas

| Formula | Meaning |
|---------|---------|
| Attention(Q,K,V) = softmax(QKᵀ/√d_k)V | Self-attention |
| s(xᵢ) = e^xᵢ / Σⱼ e^xⱼ | Softmax |
| Q=X·Wq, K=X·Wk, V=X·Wv | Q/K/V projections (all learned) |
| Max E[r(x,y)] − β·KL(policy, SFT) | PPO RLHF objective |
| MXU = 256×256 = 65,536 MACs/cycle | TPU peak |
| TPU 8t: 12.6 PFLOPs FP4, 2.7× vs Ironwood | Training variant |
| TPU 8i: 3× SRAM, 80% inference price-perf | Inference variant |
